title: Wine Wimsey Review · Oct 28
subtitle: Full Wed Oct 28 batch: 16 feed image posts (6 from your inbox + 10 new) and 4 stories · 8 Hot Mess and 8 Homebody on the feed, no TOBIs (you asked for 10 image posts) · Flags: the cat stays in the cat quote; the Walmart quote has no bra shown · the inbox menopause nap was a repeat of Tuesday #1 so I skipped it · the new quotes and stories are written fresh and checked against the used list

posts.quote: It’s actually crazy how you grow up thinking home-cooked meals every day are just normal, then get older and realise how much time and effort it took your Mom to make that happen and how lucky you were to have that.
posts.caption: My mother made dinner every single night for thirty years and never once asked for applause. I found out how much work that was around the time I tried to do it for one week. By Wednesday I was serving cereal and calling it a tradition. Now I make her soup recipe on Sundays, badly, and think of her with every stir. It never tastes quite the same, and I've decided that's the secret ingredient.
posts.first: I called her last week to ask how long the soup should simmer. She said until it smells like home. I said that's not a measurement. She laughed and said it's the only one that counts.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with pink curls tasting soup from a wooden spoon at a stove, carrots on a cutting board and a glass of red wine on the counter. Text at the top reads: It’s actually crazy how you grow up thinking home-cooked meals every day are just normal, then get older and realise how much time and effort it took your Mom to make that happen and how lucky you were to have that.

posts.quote: Going to bed used to be simple. Now I need the right pillow, the wrong pillow, three blankets, one foot sticking out, and seventeen minutes to find a position my back approves of.
posts.caption: Bedtime used to take four minutes. Now it's a production with a cast of pillows, a cooling fan, and a very specific fold of the sheet I could not explain under oath. The foot has to be out. I don't know why. My husband stopped asking years ago and just stays on his side of the line.
posts.first: Last night I finally found the perfect position and then remembered I hadn't turned off the kitchen light. I lay there for a full minute weighing the light against the position. The position won. The light is still on, and I'm at peace.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a deadpan woman in bed under three layered blankets with one bare foot sticking out, surrounded by pillows, a glass of red wine on the nightstand. Text at the top reads: Going to bed used to be simple. Now I need the right pillow, the wrong pillow, three blankets, one foot sticking out, and seventeen minutes to find a position my back approves of.

posts.quote: You’re gonna hate this, but the easiest way to organize your stuff is to throw most of it out and stop pretending you’ll need it someday.
posts.caption: I spent a full Saturday organizing the hall closet. Bins, labels, a little chart. By evening I had a very neat closet and exactly the same amount of junk, just alphabetized. Then I did the unthinkable and filled two bags for donation. It hurt for about ten minutes. After that, I could see the back wall for the first time since 2014. It's a lovely wall.
posts.first: I found a box of cords that fit nothing in this house. I kept one, because I'm not a monster, and let the rest go. So far nobody has needed them, which is exactly what I suspected.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a determined woman with pink curls putting items into a black bag in a tidy room, a donation box of clothes and stack of books beside her, a glass of red wine on a side table. Text at the top reads: You’re gonna hate this, but the easiest way to organize your stuff is to throw most of it out and stop pretending you’ll need it someday.

posts.quote: Moms did not drive us to school in a drop-off line. We walked a mile or more with our friends, carrying our books in our arms, no matter the weather.
posts.caption: We walked to school in rain, sun and one memorable sleet storm, with a bag lunch swinging from our fingers and no one checking whether we arrived. We argued about who had the best sneakers, traded stickers and got home just as the streetlights came on. It took us forever and none of us minded. I still think those were the best mornings I ever had.
posts.first: I drove past my old school last month and slowed down at the corner where we used to wait for Denise. A line of cars sat idling at the curb. I just smiled and kept going. My feet still remember the route.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a smiling woman walking along an autumn sidewalk carrying a stack of books and a travel mug, a school building and a line of cars in the background. Text at the top reads: Moms did not drive us to school in a drop-off line. We walked a mile or more with our friends, carrying our books in our arms, no matter the weather.

posts.quote: Why do people say slept like a baby? Babies wake up every two hours crying. I want to sleep like my cat: 14 hours, no responsibilities, zero regrets.
posts.caption: My cat sleeps through thunderstorms, vacuum cleaners and my phone alarm, and wakes up looking refreshed and slightly offended. I have studied her technique carefully. It involves a warm spot, a total lack of guilt, and no plans. I'm working on the second one.
posts.first: Yesterday I found her curled on my side of the bed with my pillow tucked under her chin. I stood there, holding my wine, thinking about all the choices that led us here. I slept on the couch. She did not apologize.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a tired woman with pink curls propped up in bed beside a sleeping gray tabby cat curled on the blanket, a glass of red wine on the nightstand. Text at the top reads: Why do people say slept like a baby? Babies wake up every two hours crying. I want to sleep like my cat: 14 hours, no responsibilities, zero regrets.

posts.quote: Bra off, jammies on, hair up—I call that relaxing, while others call it going to Walmart.
posts.caption: There are two kinds of people at the store after eight p.m., the ones in real clothes and the ones in flannel with a bun on top. I know which tribe I belong to. We nod at each other in the cereal aisle like members of a secret society. It's the closest thing to a club I've ever joined.
posts.first: Last week I saw a woman in a bathrobe and rain boots comparing paper towels. We locked eyes. Neither of us said a word. It was one of the most meaningful moments I've had all year.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a relaxed woman lounging on a green couch in pajamas and a robe with her hair up, holding a mug, a shopping bag and a glass of red wine beside her. Text at the top reads: Bra off, jammies on, hair up—I call that relaxing, while others call it going to Walmart.

posts.quote: I asked the universe for a calm, relaxing weekend. It heard “surprise me with three errands and a flat tire.”
posts.caption: Saturday started with a plan: coffee, a good book, absolutely nothing else. By nine I had a flat tire, a dead phone and a list of errands that multiplied overnight. The book is still on the counter. I did get to know my tire guy very well. He's a lovely man and he knows my name.
posts.first: After the tire got fixed I sat in the parking lot with a drive-through coffee and decided that was my relaxing weekend. It lasted eleven minutes. It was a good eleven minutes, and I'm counting it.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a resigned woman standing beside a car with a flat tire holding grocery bags and a phone, a glass of red wine on the car roof. Text at the top reads: I asked the universe for a calm, relaxing weekend. It heard “surprise me with three errands and a flat tire.”

posts.quote: Why does a nap feel so much better when it’s accidental?
posts.caption: I sat down with a book and told myself I'd read one chapter. The next thing I knew the room was dim, the cushion had left a pattern on my cheek and the book was on the floor. Best sleep I've had all week. The planned ones never feel that good, and I have stopped asking why.
posts.first: My husband tiptoed past and whispered that dinner was handled. I haven't felt that taken care of in years. I've decided to read one chapter every afternoon and see how far I get.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with pink curls dozing in an armchair with a book open on her chest and a blanket over her knees, a glass of red wine on the side table. Text at the top reads: Why does a nap feel so much better when it’s accidental?

posts.quote: I put my phone down for ten whole minutes and felt so proud, then picked it up to tell someone about it.
posts.caption: The screen time report came in on Sunday morning, uninvited and honest. I'm choosing to enjoy the quiet, mostly because the charger is in the other room.
posts.first: This afternoon I left my phone upstairs and went out to water the plants. I felt strangely free for about six minutes. Then I remembered I wanted to look something up and walked back inside like I had been called home.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman in a striped shirt and vest sitting on a couch with a proud smirk, reaching for a phone on the coffee table, a mug and a glass of red wine beside it. Text at the top reads: I put my phone down for ten whole minutes and felt so proud, then picked it up to tell someone about it.

posts.quote: Autumn evenings were made for a lap blanket, something simmering on the stove, and a calendar with absolutely nothing on it.
posts.caption: There is a particular kind of quiet that shows up around five o'clock in October. The light turns gold, the house smells like onions and thyme, and the whole world seems to agree it's time to slow down. I hold on to that feeling as long as I can, usually with both hands and a very warm blanket.
posts.first: Last night I turned off every light except the one over the stove and just stood there listening to the pot bubble. My husband walked in, looked around, and quietly went to find his own blanket. Marriage is mostly knowing when to join in.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a content woman with pink curls in an armchair under a knitted lap blanket with a glass of red wine, a steaming pot on the stove behind her, golden autumn light. Text at the top reads: Autumn evenings were made for a lap blanket, something simmering on the stove, and a calendar with absolutely nothing on it.

posts.quote: I'm not late. I'm just running on a schedule that nobody else has been told about yet.
posts.caption: I have a theory that time moves faster between the front door and the car. Everyone is very patient with me. I think it's pity, but I'll take it.
posts.first: I told my friend I was five minutes away and she laughed out loud, which felt rude. Then I remembered I was still standing in my kitchen looking for my keys. I found them in my hand.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a flustered woman rushing out her front door with a half-on coat, keys in her mouth and a coffee in hand, a glass of red wine left on the hallway table. Text at the top reads: I'm not late. I'm just running on a schedule that nobody else has been told about yet.

posts.quote: The best part of getting older is realizing I never have to go to a party that starts after seven.
posts.caption: I used to think the night was young. Now I check the invitation for an end time before I check the date. If it says nine, I send a heartfelt apology and a lovely dessert. Everyone is delighted and I'm in my robe by eight with the heater on. It feels like cheating the system, and I love it.
posts.first: My neighbor invited us to something that began at 8:30 and I said we'd see what we could do. My husband laughed so hard he had to sit down. We both know exactly what we'll be doing, and it involves a couch.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with pink curls relaxing with her slippers up on an ottoman, holding a party invitation with a big X, a glass of red wine beside her. Text at the top reads: The best part of getting older is realizing I never have to go to a party that starts after seven.

posts.quote: I’ve reached the stage of life where the best compliment is “you look rested.”
posts.caption: There was a time I wanted to hear that I looked young or glamorous. Now I'll take rested. Rested means I slept and nobody called before seven.
posts.first: Someone at church told me I looked rested last Sunday. I thanked her with real feeling and floated through the whole service. I'd been up until 11:40 watching a baking show. It was the right kind of lie.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman in a robe smiling at her reflection in a bathroom mirror, one hand on her cheek, a glass of red wine on the sink edge. Text at the top reads: I’ve reached the stage of life where the best compliment is “you look rested.”

posts.quote: I save the good towels for guests, then wonder why my own towels feel like sandpaper.
posts.caption: Somewhere in my linen closet is a stack of thick fluffy towels that no one has ever touched. They're saved for company, for a rainy day, for a future me who has her life together. Meanwhile we dry off with something that could sand a deck. I'm starting to think the future me is already here and deserves better.
posts.first: This morning I took one of the good towels out and used it myself. It felt like a small act of rebellion. My husband noticed and said nothing, which means he approves. We're a quietly rebellious household.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with pink curls hugging a stack of fluffy towels with a guilty grin in a bathroom, a thin old towel on the rack, a glass of red wine on the tub edge. Text at the top reads: I save the good towels for guests, then wonder why my own towels feel like sandpaper.

posts.quote: My body now predicts rain better than the weather channel, and with a lot more complaining.
posts.caption: Every joint I own has joined the forecasting team. The left shoulder handles storms, the right knee does drizzle, and they agree on nothing except the need for a chair.
posts.first: I told my friend it would rain by noon and she looked at the clear blue sky like I'd lost my mind. At 11:40 the clouds rolled in. She's asked me for the forecast every morning since. I charge in coffee.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman on her porch holding her shoulder and back with a knowing look, storm clouds gathering over autumn trees, an umbrella on the railing, a glass of red wine on a table. Text at the top reads: My body now predicts rain better than the weather channel, and with a lot more complaining.

posts.quote: A slow Sunday, a warm kitchen, and a casserole dish older than my kids. That's my idea of luxury.
posts.caption: My mother's casserole dish has a chip on one handle and a stain nobody can name. It has gone through three decades of potlucks, funerals, and Tuesday nights. Everything tastes a little better coming out of it. I'm convinced the dish knows things, and I would never dream of replacing it.
posts.first: Yesterday I pulled it out for a simple pasta bake and my son asked if he could have it someday. I said we would discuss it in my will. He took that very seriously and washed it by hand.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with pink curls pulling a bubbling casserole out of the oven with floral mitts in a warm kitchen, a glass of red wine on the counter. Text at the top reads: A slow Sunday, a warm kitchen, and a casserole dish older than my kids. That's my idea of luxury.
